A2.text:
Lala is nineteen. Last spring, her mother wanted her to do a first aid course. “Why?” Lala asked. “Better safe than sorry,” her mother said. So Lala did the course.

In June, the family went for a picnic in the mountains near Quba. Her little cousin Murad, who is nine, climbed on some big rocks by the river.

Suddenly, Murad fell. He hit his leg on a stone. There was a big cut, and it was bleeding a lot.

Everybody began to panic. Aunt Gulnar cried. Uncle Rauf shouted, “What do we do?”

But Lala remembered her course. She knew she must keep a cool head. “Give me a clean towel,” she said calmly. She pressed the towel on the cut to stop the bleeding. She told Murad, “Look at me. Breathe slowly. You are okay.”

Then she called 103. “It is an emergency,” she said. “A boy has a bad injury on his leg.” There was no phone signal on the road, so she sent their location.

An hour later, the ambulance came. The rescue team took Murad to the hospital in Quba. The doctor said, “This girl did everything right.”

Murad needed eight stitches, but he will recover. Two weeks later, he was running again.

“That was a close call,” Uncle Rauf said. Lala's mother just smiled.

B1.text:
When Lala's mother signed her up for a weekend first aid course last spring, Lala complained for days. “I'm studying architecture, not medicine,” she said. “When will I ever need it?”

“Better safe than sorry,” her mother replied, and that was the end of the discussion.

In June, the whole family drove to the forests near Quba for a picnic by the river. While the adults were busy with the kebabs, Lala's nine-year-old cousin Murad climbed onto a group of wet rocks to look at the waterfall.

Nobody saw him slip. They only heard the scream. When they reached him, he was lying between two stones with a deep cut below his knee, bleeding heavily.

In seconds, everyone was in a state of panic. Aunt Gulnar was crying, and Uncle Rauf was shouting at everyone to call someone.

Then Lala remembered something from the course: the most useful thing in an emergency is to keep a cool head. “Uncle Rauf, I need a clean towel and the water bottle,” she said firmly. She knelt beside Murad, cleaned the area and pressed the folded towel hard against the wound. “Look at me, Murad. Breathe with me. In… and out. You're doing well.”

With her other hand, she gave her phone to her aunt. “Call 103. Say it's a child with a leg injury and heavy bleeding. Send them our location.” There was almost no signal by the river, so her aunt had to climb the hill to make the call.

The ambulance couldn't get down the forest road, so the rescue team walked the last few hundred metres with a stretcher. At the hospital in Quba, the doctor examined the wound and turned to the family. “Whoever stopped that bleeding did exactly the right thing.”

Murad needed eight stitches and a week on the sofa, but he was expected to recover completely.

Driving home, Uncle Rauf shook his head. “That was a close call.”

From the front seat, Lala's mother said nothing. She didn't need to.

B2.text:
When Lala's mother enrolled her in a weekend first aid course last spring, Lala treated it as a minor act of tyranny. “I'm an architecture student,” she protested. “Under what circumstances will I ever need to bandage anyone?”

“Better safe than sorry,” her mother said, in the tone that ends negotiations, and Lala spent two Saturdays practising compressions on a plastic dummy.

That June, the extended family drove up into the forests near Quba for a riverside picnic. While the adults argued over the correct thickness of kebab meat, Lala's nine-year-old cousin Murad clambered onto a cluster of moss-covered rocks for a better view of the waterfall.

Nobody saw him slip; they only heard the scream. By the time they reached him, he was wedged between two boulders with a deep gash below his knee, bleeding alarmingly.

Within seconds the scene had dissolved into panic. Aunt Gulnar was sobbing, Uncle Rauf was ordering everyone to call someone without specifying whom or how, and the smaller children, sensing catastrophe, began to wail in sympathy.

Lala's pulse was hammering, yet a sentence from her instructor surfaced with surprising clarity: in an emergency, your first job is to keep a cool head. “Uncle Rauf — a clean towel and the water bottle, please,” she said, more evenly than she felt. Kneeling beside Murad, she rinsed the wound, folded the towel into a firm pad and pressed down hard. “Murad, eyes on me. Breathe with me — in… and out. You're being incredibly brave.”

With her free hand, she passed her phone to her aunt. “Ring 103. Say it's a child with a leg injury and heavy bleeding, and send our location.” There was barely any signal in the valley, so Gulnar had to scramble halfway up the slope to get through.

The ambulance couldn't negotiate the forest track, so the rescue crew covered the final stretch on foot with a stretcher. At the hospital in Quba, the doctor inspected the wound, then turned to the anxious family. “Whoever controlled that bleeding,” he said, “did precisely what needed to be done.”

Murad required eight stitches and a week of enforced rest on the sofa, but the doctor expected him to recover fully.

On the drive home, Uncle Rauf exhaled heavily. “That,” he said, “was a close call.”

In the front passenger seat, Lala's mother maintained a dignified silence. Some victories, after all, speak for themselves.
